sections.h2: Selling a house in Upper Dublin
sections.html:
Upper Dublin is a first-class township in Montgomery County, covering 13.3 square miles north of Philadelphia, with 26,665 residents at the 2020 census. It was farmland until the 1950s, then filled in with postwar subdivisions, so many houses are mid-century builds with the maintenance that comes with them.

Many addresses use a mailing name other than Upper Dublin: Ambler, Dresher, Fort Washington, Jarrettown and Maple Glen, with small slices of Abington, Ardsley, North Hills, Oreland and Willow Grove. They use ZIP codes 19001, 19002, 19025, 19034, 19038, 19075 and 19090, and none of them is a separate municipality. Property records and tax bills go through the township and county regardless of the postal name.

The Fort Washington Office Park, at a Pennsylvania Turnpike interchange, is the township's main job center. For a seller in Maple Glen or Fort Washington, a short commute to it is an easy point to make in a listing.

Upper Dublin has a point-of-sale process. Every property being sold must submit a Property Transfer Application under Ordinance 10-1228. The steps run alongside your sale, so start early.

  • A township official inspects the exterior for sidewalk compliance and correct house numbering. Anything found must be fixed before the sale.
  • The property file is checked for open permits. Every open permit must be finalized before the sale.
  • The file is also reviewed for zoning hearings tied to the property.
  • You sign an affidavit that smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and sump pumps are present.
  • Open Notices of Violation must be resolved before the sale.
  • Curbs and aprons are inspected and documented. A failed curb or apron does not stop the sale, but it is marked for replacement under the property maintenance code.

Permits and applications go through the township's online OpenGov portal at upperdublin.net/permits. Paper applications are no longer available, so file everything there. Leave time for both the inspection and any sidewalk repair it turns up.

sections.h2: Storm repairs, flooding and open permits
sections.html:
Nearly all of the township drains through Wissahickon Creek into the Schuylkill River, with only small corners draining to Neshaminy Creek and Pennypack Creek, so low lots near those streams deserve a closer look. An EF2 tornado from the remnants of Hurricane Ida struck the Fort Washington and Maple Glen areas on September 1, 2021, and buyers sometimes ask about repairs from that storm.

If your house had storm repairs, keep the permits, invoices and final inspection records together. Every open permit must be closed out before the sale, so storm-era work that never received a final inspection is the kind of thing that stops a closing. The township's Code Enforcement department can tell you which permits on your address are still open.

Ask for a copy of the property file before you list. It also shows past zoning hearings tied to the address, which the township reviews at transfer.

The Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds lists the realty transfer tax at 2 percent. Pennsylvania's share is 1 percent, and the rest is local. Both parties to a deed are jointly responsible to the state, so decide in the contract who pays.

If your deed shows no price, as with some family transfers, ask the Recorder how the county's common level ratio applies. Transfers claiming an exemption record with a REV-183 form from the Department of Revenue.

Assessments are county business. The Montgomery County Board of Assessment Appeals sets August 1 as the filing deadline for annual appeals, and the same date applies to exemption applications under 53 Pa.C.S. § 8844(c)(2). Annual appeals must be decided by October 31 so that new values reach taxing districts by November 15. Appeals are mailed to the Board at P.O. Box 311, Norristown, or hand-delivered during office hours.

Postmarks can lag. The county tells filers to ask for a hand cancellation, a certificate of mailing, registered or certified mail, or postage purchased at the counter. The Board also posts homestead forms, an exemption application and a "Taxing Authorities" document that names the school district and other taxing bodies for each address.

If you are behind on taxes, the Tax Claim Bureau holds an upset sale each September and December of parcels whose taxes from two years earlier remain unpaid. Buyers at an upset sale take on all liens, and the Bureau advertises each property beforehand. Paying the delinquent bill first, or selling before your parcel is listed, keeps the house out of that sale.

sections.h2: Selling with open items on the house
sections.html:
Delays in Upper Dublin often trace back to the township file. A closing agent cannot finish until permits are final, violation notices are cleared and the sidewalk is sound. Walk the front of the house and the curb yourself first. Check that the house number is visible, that sidewalk squares are level, and that smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and the sump pump are all in place.

Then call Code Enforcement and ask what the file shows. Bring the permit numbers for any deck, basement finish or roof work, and ask for the inspection history so you know which approvals are missing before a buyer's agent does. If a repair is needed, schedule it right away, since the inspection and any sidewalk work take time and the sale cannot close until they are done.

sections.h2: What are my options if I need to sell fast?
sections.html:
You can list, sell privately, or take a cash offer from a buyer who buys houses as-is. The township's transfer requirements apply to each route, so the real question is who finishes the paperwork and how soon.

  • List when open permits are closed, the sidewalk is sound and the house shows well.
  • Choose a cash sale when you inherited the house, face repairs, or have a closing date to meet. Confirm the buyer will handle the sidewalk, permit and affidavit steps with you.

Whichever route you choose, call Code Enforcement first, get the property file, and make sure the 2 percent transfer tax is set out in writing.

faqs.q: Does Upper Dublin require an inspection to sell a house?
faqs.a: Yes. Every property sold must file a Property Transfer Application, and a township official inspects the exterior for sidewalks and house numbers. Open permits and open violations must be cleared before the sale, and you sign an affidavit about smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors and sump pumps.

faqs.q: What is the transfer tax in Upper Dublin?
faqs.a: The Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds lists the realty transfer tax at 2 percent, which includes the state's 1 percent. Both buyer and seller are liable under state law, so the sales contract should say who pays.

faqs.q: When is the deadline to appeal an assessment in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: August 1 each year for annual appeals. The same deadline applies to exemption applications, and the Board advises hand delivery or a post office counter postmark.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Upper Dublin house that has open permits?
faqs.a: Not until the permits are finalized. The township's transfer review checks the property file, and every open permit must be closed before the sale, so schedule the missing inspections first.

faqs.q: What happens if I do not pay my property taxes before selling?
faqs.a: Unpaid taxes become a lien and can lead to a Tax Claim Bureau sale. The Bureau runs an upset sale each September and December for parcels with taxes unpaid from two years earlier, and buyers there take on the liens.
